value.overview: The Yellow-winged Tanager (Thraupis abbas) is a medium-sized Neotropical tanager recognized by its dusky blue-gray and olive body, pale lavender head and underparts, and bright yellow wing patches. It is mainly associated with humid and semi-open woodland, forest edges, plantations, gardens, and second-growth vegetation. Most of its established range lies in southern Mexico and northern Central America. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce and recently recorded species, especially in the northern part of the country.
value.classification: The Yellow-winged Tanager belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the passerine order Passeriformes. It is closely related to other blue, gray, and olive tanagers in the genus Thraupis.
value.identification: Adults are about 16–18 cm long. The head, throat, and breast are pale lavender or bluish gray, while the back and body are darker olive or blue-gray. The wings and tail are dusky, with conspicuous yellow patches on the wings that are especially noticeable in flight or when the bird spreads its wings. Juveniles are duller and more olive-green, lacking much of the adult’s bluish and lavender coloration. The Blue-gray Tanager is a possible confusion species but lacks the distinctive yellow wing patches.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from eastern and southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua, with the range extending into western Panama according to some modern treatments. In Costa Rica, it is not a widespread or regularly common resident; records have been concentrated in the northern lowlands, including the Los Chiles area, with additional observations suggesting occurrence near the northern Caribbean plain and adjacent foothills. It uses humid forest edges, second growth, plantations, gardens, clearings, and other semi-open habitats, generally from lowlands to about 1,500–1,800 m.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. It may make short local movements in response to fruit availability. In Costa Rica, its occurrence appears localized and irregular rather than representing a broad, well-established seasonal migration.
value.breeding: The Yellow-winged Tanager builds a small open cup nest from fibers, dry leaves, twigs, and moss, usually placed in a tree or shrub at moderate height. Available accounts report clutches of about three grayish eggs marked with brown. Both adults are associated with nest construction and care of young, although detailed information on incubation, nesting dates, and breeding success is limited. Confirmed breeding information from Costa Rica is particularly scarce, so the species’ local breeding status there remains insufficiently documented.
value.dietFeeding: It is an omnivorous canopy and edge-forager that takes a mixture of small fruits, berries, figs, nectar, and insects. Birds usually search among foliage and outer branches, sometimes taking insects from vegetation or in short flights. Fruit-bearing trees can attract pairs or groups, and the species may forage in gardens, plantations, and other modified habitats when suitable food is available.
value.behavior: Yellow-winged Tanagers are active, social birds that may occur in pairs, family groups, or larger flocks, especially where food is concentrated. Their calls are high-pitched and sibilant, and they may call while perched or flying. They commonly move through forest borders, clearings, and second-growth vegetation, often remaining in the middle or upper levels of trees. Their tolerance of semi-open habitats may help them persist in landscapes altered by agriculture and settlement.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species has a broad range and is generally regarded as common to locally common in much of its established distribution. Its status in Costa Rica is less certain because records are relatively sparse and the species appears to be uncommon or localized there.
